name: Voltaire
dossier: A Philosophical Dictionary, volume 1, is quoted from William F. Fleming's translation in the 1901 Works of Voltaire. Only the articles from A through Apparition are searched. Later volumes are not in this index.
voice: I ask who is harmed, and who is paying the executioner.

works.title: A Philosophical Dictionary, volume 1
works.note: Project Gutenberg ebook 35621, from The Works of Voltaire, E. R. DuMont, 1901

entries.claim: It was most probably by mutual traffic which administered to their wants, that society was first established among men; and it is necessary that those between whom commerce is carried on should understand one another.
entries.loc: A, B, C, OR ALPHABET., paragraph 7
entries.bears: This article guesses that society began in traffic that served people's wants.

entries.claim: A true Epicurean was mild, moderate, just, amiable--a man of whom no society had to complain--one who did not pay executioners to assassinate in public those who thought differently from himself.
entries.bears: The true Epicurean is described as mild and just, and as someone who does not hire executioners for opinions.

entries.claim: "The worthy administrators of justice," said he, "are like a cat set to take care of a cheese, lest it should be gnawed by the mice.
entries.bears: A speaker in the article compares administrators of justice to a cat set to guard a cheese.

entries.claim: It is but too true that one fanatic is sufficient for the commission of a parricide, without any accomplice.
entries.bears: One fanatic, he says, is enough for a parricide, with no accomplice required.

entries.claim: In short, he knows little of the human mind who does not know that fanaticism renders the populace capable of anything.
entries.bears: Fanaticism is said to make a populace capable of anything.

entries.claim: The alphabet article guesses that society began when people traded to meet their wants and so had to understand one another.
entries.loc: A, B, C, or the Alphabet
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. Society is tied to mutual traffic, not to a single doctrine.

entries.claim: A true Epicurean is described as mild, moderate, and just, and as a man who does not pay executioners to kill people for a different opinion.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The moral praise is for mildness and for refusing public killing over opinions.

entries.claim: The anecdotes say that one fanatic is enough to commit a parricide, and that fanaticism makes a populace capable of anything.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The dictionary treats fanaticism as a public danger, not as a private taste.
